\section{EC-HTE: Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects}
\label{sec:method}

EC-HTE corrects subgroup-level misclassification bias in three stages: estimate per-subgroup confusion matrices via hierarchical Bayes, invert them to correct observed outcome moments, and propagate correction uncertainty into downstream causal estimators.
The complete procedure is summarized in Algorithm~\ref{alg:echte} (Appendix~\ref{app:algorithm}).

\subsection{Hierarchical Bayes Confusion Matrix Estimation}

We place a Dirichlet-Multinomial hierarchical model over the confusion matrices $\{C_s\}_{s=1}^K$.
For each subgroup $s$, row $j$ of $C_s$ has a Dirichlet prior $\text{Dir}(\alpha_0 \cdot \mathbf{e}_j)$, where $\mathbf{e}_j$ is the $j$-th standard basis vector and $\alpha_0 > 0$ is a shared concentration parameter.
A $\text{Gamma}(3, 1)$ hyperprior on $\alpha_0$ controls the strength of partial pooling across subgroups: large $\alpha_0$ pulls subgroup estimates toward the identity matrix (low error), while small $\alpha_0$ allows subgroup-specific rates to dominate.
This partial pooling implements a James-Stein shrinkage effect, borrowing strength across subgroups to reduce variance for small subgroups while preserving heterogeneity where the data support it.

Posterior inference uses a Gibbs sampler with 4 chains, 4000 iterations (2000 warmup).
We require convergence diagnostics $\hat{R} < 1.01$ and effective sample size $\text{ESS} > 845$ for all parameters before accepting estimates.
In practice, all runs achieve $\hat{R} < 1.0034$ and $\text{ESS} > 1618$, well within these thresholds.
HB estimation outperforms stratified MLE in 87.5\% of configurations (21 of 24) across the experimental grid (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}), with the largest gains when $n_{\text{expert}} / K < 100$.
The advantage requires at least $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ per subgroup; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred because the hierarchical model lacks sufficient observations for stable shrinkage.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics.
Sensitivity analysis shows $<$5\% RMSE variation under 2$\times$ hyperprior perturbation, confirming that results are not driven by prior specification.

\subsection{Subgroup-Stratified Correction}

Given posterior mean confusion matrices $\hat{C}_s$, we correct observed outcome moments per subgroup by matrix inversion:
\begin{equation}
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = \hat{C}_s^{-1} \cdot \hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s,
\end{equation}
where $\hat{\boldsymbol{\mu}}_s = [\hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(0, s),\, \hat{\tau}_{\text{obs}}(1, s)]^\top$ collects the observed conditional outcome moments in subgroup $s$.
This requires $\det(\hat{C}_s) \neq 0$ for all $s$, which holds under assumption~(A4) ($\pi_s \neq 0.5$) but may fail in finite samples when error rates approach degeneracy.
In practice, Laplace smoothing of the confusion matrix counts ensures finite-sample invertibility.
We impose a singularity guard: if the condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s) > 100$, subgroup $s$ falls back to global correction $\bar{C}^{-1}$ rather than risk numerical instability from near-singular inversion.

The contrast with global correction is direct.
Global correction applies $\bar{C}^{-1}$ uniformly to all subgroups, introducing the $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau$ bias identified in Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}.
Subgroup-stratified correction eliminates this bias by matching each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification structure, at the cost of higher variance from estimating $K$ separate confusion matrices (Section~\ref{sec:budget}).

\subsection{Variance-Adjusted CausalForest}

For heterogeneous treatment effect estimation, we feed corrected covariates into CausalForestDML~\cite{wager2018causal} with honest splitting.
The forest produces per-observation standard error estimates $\text{se}_i$.
To account for confusion matrix correction, we propagate uncertainty through the inverse mapping:
\begin{equation}
\text{se}_{\text{corrected},i} = \sqrt{\text{diag}\!\left(\hat{C}_{S_i}^{-1}\, \text{diag}(\text{se}_i^2)\, \hat{C}_{S_i}^{-\top}\right)}.
\end{equation}
This is a plug-in approach: the standard errors reflect outcome variance conditional on $\hat{C}_s$ but do not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, the plug-in approximation is reasonable because confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance.
Below this threshold, the standard errors may understate total uncertainty; this limitation is discussed further in the Limitations section.

\paragraph{Diagnostic criterion.}
As a practical corollary of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}, the product $|\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau|$ serves as a computable diagnostic for whether global correction will harm specific subgroups.
The bias decomposition identity predicts that bias is proportional to this product, and both quantities can be estimated from a modest pilot sample (we use $n_{\text{expert}} = 50$ in our experiments).
A threshold calibrated via leave-one-out cross-validation achieves AUC~=~0.83 at the subgroup level (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
The recommended workflow is: compute the diagnostic from pilot data; if any subgroup shows a large product, apply EC-HTE; if the product is uniformly small, global correction suffices.

\paragraph{Composition with PPCI.}
EC-HTE corrects structured covariate misclassification through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ inversion but cannot address outcome-level measurement error.
PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects residual outcome bias using a debiasing estimator but assumes correct covariate labels.
The two methods are complementary: apply EC-HTE first to correct covariate labels, then PPCI to correct outcome predictions.
Neither is redundant with the other: EC-HTE alone cannot fix outcome error, while PPCI alone incurs higher variance for covariate error.
Under both error types simultaneously, the composition reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 (Section~\ref{sec:ppci}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Measurement error and annotation models.}
Classical measurement error theory shows that correction via estimated error models can amplify MSE when the error structure is misspecified~\cite{fuller1987measurement,carroll2006measurement}; Bayesian approaches require informative priors when identification is weak~\cite{gustafson2003measurement}, and nonparametric methods use repeated measurements or instruments to recover the true distribution~\cite{hu2008nonparametric}.
We formalize this principle for a specific causal estimand: Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} gives an exact identity for CATE bias under global correction with heterogeneous misclassification.
\citet{battistin2014treatment} study treatment effect estimation with covariate measurement error but focus on average effects and identification conditions rather than subgroup-level heterogeneity.
In the annotation literature, \citet{dawid1979maximum} introduced confusion matrix estimation for multiple annotators, with extensions to item difficulty, annotator competence, and hierarchical priors~\cite{passonneau2014benefits,hovy2013learning,paun2018comparing}.
Our hierarchical estimator (Section~\ref{sec:method}) adapts this architecture from label aggregation to causal inference, tying the prior structure to the subgroup dimension that defines treatment effect heterogeneity.

\paragraph{HTE estimation and LLM annotation error.}
Causal forests~\cite{athey2016recursive,wager2018causal}, double/debiased ML~\cite{chernozhukov2018dml}, doubly-robust CATE estimators~\cite{kennedy2023dr}, and meta-learners~\cite{kunzel2019metalearners} all assume that covariates defining heterogeneity are observed without error; when the effect modifier is misclassified, CATE estimates conflate effects across groups.
EC-HTE provides upstream correction that restores valid inputs to any downstream estimator.
The corrected pseudo-outcomes are in principle compatible with other HTE estimators such as the R-learner~\citep{nie2021quasi}.
LLMs now match crowd-worker accuracy on many classification tasks~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp,pangakis2023automated}, but \citet{ashwin2025bias} show that error rates vary by up to $5\times$ across demographic subgroups.
This subgroup-varying error is the failure mode we address: it distorts the very contrasts that define the research question, and prior work documents the pattern without providing a correction mechanism for downstream causal estimands.

\paragraph{Prediction-powered and design-based correction.}
PPI~\cite{angelopoulos2023ppi,zrnic2024cross} and DSL~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates assuming homogeneous prediction error.
Applied per-subgroup, DSL operates at the estimand level without cross-subgroup borrowing, yielding strictly higher variance than EC-HTE's measurement-model approach (confusion matrix inversion with hierarchical shrinkage).
\citet{mozer2026ppi} extend PPI to arm-specific ATE correction; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} targets conditional estimands but corrects outcome-side error ($\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$), not covariate-side misclassification; ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} targets the outcome model rather than the heterogeneity structure.
None corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the effect modifier indexing the CATE function.
\citet{imai2010causal} study treatment misclassification, requiring instrumental variables or partial identification; our problem is structurally distinct because the treatment is observed correctly but the effect modifier is misclassified, admitting exact correction through confusion matrices rather than bounds.
Extended discussion of these distinctions appears in Appendix~\ref{app:related}.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

Large language models (LLMs) now routinely replace human annotators in computational social science (CSS), producing labels for sentiment, hate speech, stance, and political discourse at costs orders of magnitude below manual coding~\cite{gilardi2023chatgpt,tornberg2024chatgpt,ziems2024nlp}.
Yet these annotations are not uniformly accurate.
\citet{ashwin2025bias} document that LLM misclassification rates vary by up to 5$\times$ across demographic subgroups defined by refugee status, gender, and education level.
In a pilot study, GPT-4.1 achieves 85.8\% binary accuracy on TweetEval sentiment, but error rates range from 10.2\% to 20.0\% across text-feature subgroups ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), confirming that misclassification heterogeneity is not a theoretical abstraction.
The pilot confirms that the heterogeneity levels assumed in our synthetic DGPs ($\Delta\pi = 0.05$--$0.20$) fall within the empirically observed range ($\Delta\pi = 0.098$), supporting the practical relevance of our parameter space.
When such annotations serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis, subgroup-specific errors propagate directly into conditional average treatment effect (CATE) estimates.
The resulting bias is not random noise that averages out; it is structured by the same demographic axes that define the research question.
Standard correction procedures, which estimate a single confusion matrix and apply its inverse uniformly, cannot account for this heterogeneity.

We formalize this problem and discover a previously unrecognized bias mechanism.
When a pooled confusion matrix is applied to correct subgroup CATEs, it misattributes error across subgroups with an exact product form: the bias in subgroup $s$ equals $\delta_s \cdot \Delta\tau / (1 - 2\bar{\pi})$, where $\delta_s$ is the deviation from the pooled error rate and $\Delta\tau$ is the CATE heterogeneity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}).
This is not a bound but an exact population-level identity, verified empirically with $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$) and $R^2 = 0.974$ ($K{=}4$).
A direct consequence is that global correction can be worse than no correction at all: in 50\% of our experimental configurations, global debiasing increases absolute bias relative to the naive estimator, with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$ with CausalForest).
Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE) addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian estimation of subgroup-stratified confusion matrices combined with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.011 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$).
The bias decomposition identity also yields a computable diagnostic: the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product predicts when global correction will fail at the subgroup level (AUC = 0.83), so practitioners can decide whether stratified correction is warranted before committing to the additional expert annotation it requires.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity and expert budget; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices and EC-HTE's variance cost is not justified (Figure~\ref{fig:bias_mechanism}).

This problem matters because subgroup CATEs inform resource allocation decisions: which communities benefit most from policy interventions, where programs should be targeted, and how reforms affect different groups.
Biased CATE estimates can reverse the sign of apparent treatment heterogeneity, leading practitioners to allocate resources away from communities that benefit most.
The failure mode is subtle: a researcher who corrects for annotation noise using a pooled confusion matrix may introduce more bias than doing nothing, precisely in the low-error subgroups where original labels were most trustworthy.
As LLM annotation pipelines replace manual coding across the social sciences, heterogeneous classification errors will propagate to an increasing share of causal analyses.

Several methods address measurement error in downstream statistical analyses, but none handles the specific failure mode we identify.
Prediction-Powered Inference (PPI;~\citealt{angelopoulos2023ppi}) and Design-based Supervised Learning~\cite{egami2024dsl} correct population-level aggregates by combining predicted and gold-standard labels, assuming homogeneous prediction error across subgroups.
These methods produce valid confidence intervals for marginal quantities but do not extend to subgroup-conditional estimands.
Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI;~\citealt{sui2026ppci}) extends PPI to conditional means but targets outcome-side prediction error rather than covariate-side misclassification; it corrects $\hat{Y}$ given true $Z$, not the reverse.
\citet{mozer2026ppi} prove that arm-specific rectifiers fix average treatment effect bias under differential prediction error, but their analysis is limited to population averages and does not address heterogeneity estimation.
ForestIV~\cite{bu2023forestiv} handles ML-covariate measurement error in regression forests but targets the outcome model rather than the treatment effect heterogeneity structure.
The gap is specific: no existing method corrects bias when the mismeasured variable is the one that defines the heterogeneity structure itself, i.e., the effect modifier whose levels index the CATE function.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig1_bias_mechanism.pdf}
\caption{Bias mechanism under global vs.\ subgroup-stratified correction. Global correction applies the pooled error rate $\bar{\pi}$ uniformly, over-correcting low-error subgroups (introducing bias where none existed) and under-correcting high-error subgroups. EC-HTE matches each subgroup's correction to its own misclassification rate.}
\label{fig:bias_mechanism}
\end{figure}

Our contributions are:
\begin{itemize}
    \item A bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) showing that global confusion-matrix correction introduces bias exactly proportional to the product of error-rate heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity, including a formal condition under which debiasing increases bias (Section~\ref{sec:theory}).
    \item The EC-HTE framework: hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation combined with CausalForestDML and plug-in standard error propagation, with a singularity guard for near-degenerate subgroups (Section~\ref{sec:method}).
    \item A computable diagnostic criterion derived from Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}: the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product predicts at the subgroup level whether global correction will fail, achieving AUC = 0.83 in cross-validated evaluation (Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}).
    \item A composition of EC-HTE with PPCI for dual covariate/outcome error settings, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$, DGP~C) when both error types are present (Section~\ref{sec:ppci}).
    \item Comprehensive validation across 520 synthetic configurations (100 Monte Carlo runs each) and a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5000$), with crossover analysis ($n_{\text{expert}}{=}250$ for $K{=}2$, $n_{\text{expert}}{=}1000$ for $K{=}4$) establishing the conditions under which EC-HTE improves over global correction and where it does not (Section~\ref{sec:bias_mechanism}, Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
\end{itemize}

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).
EC-HTE maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage under up to 50\% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).

\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level.
In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{figures/fig2_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Bias amplification under global correction across the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ parameter grid ($K{=}2$). (a) Low-error subgroup: global correction always helps (ratio $< 1$). (b) High-error subgroup: when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (dashed line), global correction \emph{increases} bias relative to the naive estimator (hatched region), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), global correction already achieves low bias (0.009), and EC-HTE provides negligible improvement (0.005) at the cost of slightly higher RMSE (0.075 vs.\ 0.074).
This illustrates the conditional nature of EC-HTE's advantage: when $\Delta\pi$ is small, the variance cost of stratification is not offset by bias reduction.

In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment, the pattern shifts.
Global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023) among non-oracle methods, while HB EC-HTE attains 0.027 with substantially higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124).
This is consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and the high-error subgroups (S2, S3) comprising only 23\% of data: the bias reduction from stratification is marginal while the variance cost of four per-subgroup confusion matrices is substantial.
HB EC-HTE does improve over stratified MLE (RMSE 0.225 vs.\ 0.248), confirming that partial pooling helps, but the improvement is insufficient to overcome the structural variance from unbalanced subgroup sizes.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, HB and MLE converge to within 5\% on all metrics.

\paragraph{CausalForest K-dependence.}
When the downstream estimator is a CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, the bias mechanism operates with amplified magnitude.
At $K{=}4$/extreme/$n{=}500$, EC-HTE Forest reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 (global) to 0.040, a 4.8$\times$ improvement with dramatically better coverage (0.91 vs.\ 0.58).
The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies: global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$ in the worst subgroup, because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies the effect of label errors.
At $K{=}4$/$n{=}100$, EC-HTE Forest RMSE reaches 1.43 (3.5$\times$ naive), underscoring the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.

\subsection{Diagnostic Criterion}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

As a practical corollary of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}, the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product provides a computable diagnostic for predicting when global correction will fail.
Using leave-one-out cross-validation at the subgroup level, a threshold classifier on $|\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau|$ achieves AUC = 0.83 for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
The Pearson correlation between the signed product and the observed bias ratio is $r = 0.86$.
At the setting level (averaging across subgroups within a configuration), the diagnostic has AUC = 0.47, which is no better than random.
The diagnostic operates at the subgroup level because the product criterion identifies \emph{which subgroups} are affected rather than whether a given experimental setting is globally problematic.
In practice, the diagnostic enables researchers to identify vulnerable subgroups before committing to a correction strategy: if any subgroup has $\pi_s \ll \bar{\pi}$ and $\tau(z)$ varies across $z$-levels, global correction should be avoided.
Figure~\ref{fig:roc} (Appendix) shows the ROC curve and correlation scatter plot.

\subsection{Expert Budget Analysis}
\label{sec:budget}

The crossover point at which EC-HTE achieves lower RMSE than global correction is $n_{\text{expert}} = 250$ for $K{=}2$/extreme and $n_{\text{expert}} = 1000$ for $K{=}4$/extreme (Figure~\ref{fig:budget} in the Appendix).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.

\subsection{PPCI Complementarity}
\label{sec:ppci}

EC-HTE corrects covariate misclassification but cannot address outcome-level error; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects outcome-level error but assumes correct covariates.
Under both error types simultaneously (DGP~C), EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$), a $25\times$ improvement over EC-HTE alone (Table~\ref{tab:ppci} in the Appendix).
Under covariate error only, PPCI adds nothing; under no error, all methods perform equivalently.
The two corrections are complementary: EC-HTE handles covariate-side $M^{-1}$ inversion while PPCI handles residual outcome-level bias.

\section*{Limitations}

\paragraph{Expert budget threshold.}
EC-HTE requires at least $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for the hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage estimates to stabilize.
Below this threshold, per-subgroup confusion matrix estimates are too noisy for reliable inversion, and stratified MLE is preferred.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics, making the hierarchical model unnecessary at large expert budgets.

\paragraph{RMSE tradeoff at small $n$.}
EC-HTE achieves lower bias than global correction but incurs higher variance when the expert budget is small relative to the number of subgroups.
In the most unfavorable configuration ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$), EC-HTE CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
Practitioners should weigh whether bias or variance is more consequential for their application before adopting subgroup-stratified correction at small sample sizes.

\paragraph{Baseline classifier quality.}
EC-HTE additionally requires that the baseline classifier achieve moderate accuracy; when overall misclassification exceeds ${\sim}50$\% (as in our hate speech case study, Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}), confusion matrix inversion amplifies noise and correction becomes underpowered.

\paragraph{Plug-in standard errors.}
The variance-adjusted CausalForest propagates outcome uncertainty through the inverse confusion matrix $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ but does not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
This plug-in approximation is reasonable at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, where confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance, but may understate total uncertainty below this threshold.
Full Bayesian propagation of confusion matrix posterior uncertainty through the causal forest splitting procedure is computationally prohibitive and left to future work.

\paragraph{Symmetric misclassification assumption.}
All main experiments use symmetric error rates ($P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}0) = P(\hat{Z}{=}0 \mid Z{=}1)$).
Real LLM annotators typically exhibit asymmetric confusion patterns ($\text{FPR}_s \neq \text{FNR}_s$).
The bias decomposition generalizes: since the global and subgroup mixing matrices are both row-stochastic, the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
Empirical validation across three asymmetric configurations confirms $R^2 = 0.991$ and EC-HTE achieves $4\times$ bias reduction, suggesting the symmetric assumption is expository rather than fundamental.

\paragraph{Additive CATE structure.}
Our semi-synthetic DGPs use additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives from the confusion matrix structure and holds for arbitrary outcome models; under multiplicative or interaction-based CATE structures, the practical magnitude of the bias depends on how the outcome model affects $\Delta\tau$.

\paragraph{Subgroup structure assumed known.}
EC-HTE requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups as input.
Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require fundamentally different approaches.
The hierarchical prior provides partial robustness to noisy subgroup definitions through automatic shrinkage toward the global mean, but intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ budget threshold, limiting practical applicability to settings with moderate $K$.

340	\section{Real-Data Case Study: Hate Speech Detection}
341	\label{app:hatespeech}
342	
343	We apply EC-HTE to the UC Berkeley Measuring Hate Speech corpus~\cite{kennedy2020constructing}, annotating 2{,}496 comments for dehumanization using GPT-4.1.
344	Four text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing platform (Reddit/Gab vs.\ Twitter/YouTube) and text length (above/below median), yielding balanced groups ($n \approx 624$ each).
345	
346	\paragraph{Positive finding: real-world heterogeneity.}
347	Per-subgroup misclassification rates range from 0.266 to 0.383, confirming heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi = 0.117$) in a real annotation setting.
348	At the error-type level, FPR ranges from 8.5\% to 21.3\% across text-feature subgroups, demonstrating that subgroup-varying misclassification is not an artifact of synthetic design but arises naturally in real NLP annotation tasks.
349	
350	\paragraph{Boundary condition: statistical power at extreme FNR.}
351	Correction results are inconclusive: all corrected confidence intervals contain zero, and point estimate differences between methods are not statistically significant.
352	The high baseline FNR (53.3\%) amplifies variance through matrix inversion (variance amplification factor up to 15.7$\times$), rendering the comparison underpowered.
353	When $P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}1) \approx 0.5$, the confusion matrix approaches singularity, and inversion amplifies estimation noise regardless of stratification strategy.
354	This complements the expert budget threshold identified in Section~\ref{sec:budget}: EC-HTE requires \emph{both} sufficient expert labels \emph{and} sufficient baseline classifier quality.
355	
356	\paragraph{Diagnostic connection.}
357	The diagnostic criterion ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, Section~\ref{sec:diagnostic}) identifies when correction is worthwhile under moderate baseline accuracy.
358	This case study illustrates that even when $\Delta\pi$ is large, extreme baseline error renders correction underpowered rather than beneficial.
359	A practical prerequisite is that the per-subgroup confusion matrix condition number $\kappa(\hat{C}_s)$ remain moderate; when $\kappa > 50$, as observed here, practitioners should prioritize improving annotation quality before applying any matrix-inversion-based correction.
360	
361	\section{Cross-Model Consistency}
362	\label{app:multilm}
363	
364	We evaluate whether misclassification heterogeneity is model-specific by annotating 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with six OpenAI models spanning three generations.
365	Six text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing hashtag presence and text length.
366	Spearman rank correlations of per-subgroup error rates across all six subgroups range from $\rho = 0.82$ to $1.00$ (all $p < 0.05$), indicating that the subgroup error structure is consistent across architectures.%
367	\footnote{When restricted to the four subgroups with $n \geq 10$, Spearman tests are underpowered (four ranks yield limited statistical resolution), but ranking direction remains consistent. The filtered $\Delta\pi$ values in Table~\ref{tab:multilm} serve as a robustness check independent of rank-order testing.}
368	
369	\begin{table}[t]
370	\centering
371	\caption{Effective misclassification heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi$) across six OpenAI models on TweetEval sentiment (500 tweets, filtered to 4 subgroups with $n \geq 10$).}
372	\label{tab:multilm}

374	\begin{tabular}{lcc}

376	Model & Effective $\Delta\pi$ & $> 0.05$? \\
377	\midrule
378	GPT-3.5-Turbo & 0.198 & \checkmark \\
379	GPT-4-Turbo & 0.149 & \checkmark \\
380	GPT-4o-mini & 0.136 & \checkmark \\
381	GPT-5.4 & 0.114 & \checkmark \\
382	GPT-4.1 & 0.098 & \checkmark \\
383	GPT-4o & 0.080 & \checkmark \\
384	\bottomrule
385	\end{tabular}
386	\end{table}
387	
388	All six models exhibit effective $\Delta\pi > 0.05$ on the four retained subgroups (Table~\ref{tab:multilm}), and 5 of 6 share the same worst subgroup (\texttt{True\_medium}: tweets with hashtags and medium text length).
389	Newer models reduce absolute error rates but do not eliminate subgroup heterogeneity: GPT-5.4 achieves $\Delta\pi = 0.114$ compared to GPT-3.5-Turbo's $0.198$.

\section*{Limitations}

EC-HTE requires $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for stable hierarchical Bayesian estimation; below this threshold, stratified MLE is preferred.
Even above this threshold, stratification incurs a variance cost: at $K{=}4$, extreme heterogeneity, and $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$, CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
The method also requires moderate baseline classifier accuracy; when overall misclassification exceeds ${\sim}50$\% (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}), confusion matrix inversion amplifies noise and correction becomes underpowered.

The variance-adjusted CausalForest uses a plug-in approximation: it propagates outcome uncertainty through $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ but does not propagate confusion matrix estimation uncertainty itself.
This is reasonable at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$ but may understate total uncertainty below this threshold; full Bayesian propagation is left to future work.

All main experiments use symmetric error rates and additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
The bias identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) generalizes to asymmetric confusion matrices (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}, $R^2 = 0.991$) and derives from the confusion matrix structure rather than the outcome model, though practical bias magnitude under multiplicative CATEs depends on how the outcome model affects $\Delta\tau$.
EC-HTE further requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups; continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require different approaches, and intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ budget threshold.

EC-HTE requires at least $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ per subgroup for the hierarchical Bayesian shrinkage estimates to stabilize.
Below this threshold, per-subgroup confusion matrix estimates are too noisy for reliable inversion, and stratified MLE is preferred.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$, HB and stratified MLE converge to within 0.5\% on all metrics, making the hierarchical model unnecessary at large expert budgets.

\paragraph{RMSE tradeoff at small $n$.}
EC-HTE achieves lower bias than global correction but incurs higher variance when the expert budget is small relative to the number of subgroups.
In the most unfavorable configuration ($K{=}4$, extreme, $n_{\text{expert}} \leq 100$), EC-HTE CausalForest RMSE reaches 3.5$\times$ that of the naive estimator.
Practitioners should weigh whether bias or variance is more consequential for their application before adopting subgroup-stratified correction at small sample sizes.

\paragraph{Baseline classifier quality.}
EC-HTE additionally requires that the baseline classifier achieve moderate accuracy; when overall misclassification exceeds ${\sim}50$\% (as in our hate speech case study, Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}), confusion matrix inversion amplifies noise and correction becomes underpowered.

\paragraph{Plug-in standard errors.}
The variance-adjusted CausalForest propagates outcome uncertainty through the inverse confusion matrix $\hat{C}_s^{-1}$ but does not propagate uncertainty from the confusion matrix estimation itself.
This plug-in approximation is reasonable at $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 100$, where confusion matrix estimation variance is small relative to outcome variance, but may understate total uncertainty below this threshold.
Full Bayesian propagation of confusion matrix posterior uncertainty through the causal forest splitting procedure is computationally prohibitive and left to future work.

\paragraph{Symmetric misclassification assumption.}
All main experiments use symmetric error rates ($P(\hat{Z}{=}1 \mid Z{=}0) = P(\hat{Z}{=}0 \mid Z{=}1)$).
Real LLM annotators typically exhibit asymmetric confusion patterns ($\text{FPR}_s \neq \text{FNR}_s$).
The bias decomposition generalizes: since the global and subgroup mixing matrices are both row-stochastic, the product structure persists with modified coefficients (Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
Empirical validation across three asymmetric configurations confirms $R^2 = 0.991$ and EC-HTE achieves $4\times$ bias reduction, suggesting the symmetric assumption is expository rather than fundamental.

\paragraph{Additive CATE structure.}
Our semi-synthetic DGPs use additive CATE injection ($Y(1) = Y(0) + \tau(Z)$).
Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} derives from the confusion matrix structure and holds for arbitrary outcome models; under multiplicative or interaction-based CATE structures, the practical magnitude of the bias depends on how the outcome model affects $\Delta\tau$.

\paragraph{Subgroup structure assumed known.}
EC-HTE requires discrete, pre-defined subgroups as input.
Continuous effect modifiers or latent subgroup discovery settings require fundamentally different approaches.
The hierarchical prior provides partial robustness to noisy subgroup definitions through automatic shrinkage toward the global mean, but intersectional subgroups with many levels may exceed the $n_{\text{expert}} / K \geq 25$ budget threshold, limiting practical applicability to settings with moderate $K$.

lines: We evaluate whether misclassification heterogeneity is model-specific by annotating 500 TweetEval sentiment tweets with six OpenAI models spanning three generations.
Six text-feature subgroups are defined by crossing hashtag presence and text length.

-Spearman rank correlations of per-subgroup error rates across all six subgroups range from $\rho = 0.82$ to $1.00$ (all $p < 0.05$), indicating that the subgroup error structure is consistent across architectures.%

-\footnote{When restricted to the four subgroups with $n \geq 10$, Spearman tests are underpowered (four ranks yield limited statistical resolution), but ranking direction remains consistent. \section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

We identified an exact bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) showing that global confusion-matrix correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$, the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity.
This is not a bound but an exact population-level result, and it reveals that standard debiasing worsens subgroup CATE estimates in 50\% of experimental configurations.
EC-HTE addresses this through hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified correction combined with CausalForestDML (Section~\ref{sec:method}), with a computable diagnostic (AUC $= 0.83$) that identifies when stratified correction is warranted (Section~\ref{sec:ec_hte_eval}).
Composition with PPCI handles dual covariate/outcome error, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.

The recommended workflow is straightforward: compute $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ from a modest pilot sample (we use $n_{\text{expert}} = 50$ in our experiments); if the product is large for any subgroup, apply EC-HTE with $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$ ($K{=}2$) or $\geq 1{,}000$ ($K{=}4$); if uniformly small, global correction suffices.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional, not universal.
When error heterogeneity is low, the variance cost of per-subgroup estimation outweighs the bias reduction, and global correction remains the appropriate choice.
This conditionality is a feature of the framework: the diagnostic tells practitioners when to incur the cost of stratified correction and when not to.

Our validation uses known subgroup structure and primarily symmetric misclassification,
though the product structure extends to arbitrary asymmetric confusion matrices
(Remark~2 and Appendix~\ref{app:asymmetric}).
Latent or continuous subgroup discovery, online settings with streaming annotations,
and relaxation of the conditional independence assumption are natural next steps.
As LLM annotation pipelines scale across the social sciences, the interaction between measurement error heterogeneity and causal effect heterogeneity will grow more consequential; the broader landscape of error-heterogeneity interactions in automated causal inference remains open.

1	\begin{abstract}
2	We prove that correcting LLM annotation error with a single pooled confusion matrix---standard practice when LLM labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis---introduces subgroup-level bias exactly proportional to the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$), an exact population-level identity verified at $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$).
3	In 50\% of experimental configurations, global correction worsens subgroup CATE bias, with amplification up to 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$, difference-in-means) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$, CausalForest).
4	A natural solution enabled by this insight, Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), combines hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.011 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$); a computable diagnostic ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product, AUC $= 0.83$ at the subgroup level) identifies when stratified correction is warranted.
5	Composed with Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI) for dual covariate/outcome error, the two corrections are each necessary and jointly sufficient, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.
6	EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices.
7	We validate across 520 synthetic configurations (100 Monte Carlo runs each) and a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$).
8	\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
We prove that correcting LLM annotation error with a single pooled confusion matrix---standard practice when LLM labels serve as effect modifiers in heterogeneous treatment effect (HTE) analysis---introduces subgroup-level bias exactly proportional to the product of misclassification heterogeneity and CATE heterogeneity ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$), an exact population-level identity verified at $R^2 = 0.994$ ($K{=}2$).
In 50\% of experimental configurations, global correction worsens subgroup CATE bias, with amplification up to 2.86$\times$ ($K{=}2$, difference-in-means) and 5.9$\times$ ($K{=}4$, CausalForest).
A natural solution enabled by this insight, Error-Corrected Heterogeneous Treatment Effects (EC-HTE), combines hierarchical Bayesian subgroup-stratified confusion matrix estimation with CausalForestDML, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 to 0.011 under extreme heterogeneity ($K{=}2$); a computable diagnostic ($\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product, AUC $= 0.83$ at the subgroup level) identifies when stratified correction is warranted.
Composed with Prediction-Powered Conditional Inference (PPCI) for dual covariate/outcome error, the two corrections are each necessary and jointly sufficient, reducing $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007.
EC-HTE's advantage is conditional on sufficient error heterogeneity; when $\Delta\pi$ is small, global correction suffices.
We validate across 520 synthetic configurations (100 Monte Carlo runs each) and a semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment ($N{=}5{,}000$).
\end{abstract}

content.content:
1	\section{Experiments}
2	
3	\subsection{Setup}
4	
5	We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
6	The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
7	Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
8	The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.
9	
10	We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
11	For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
12	Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
13	Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
14	The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).
15	EC-HTE maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage under up to 50\% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).
16	
17	\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
18	\label{sec:bias_mechanism}
19	
20	The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
21	We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
22	Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level.
23	In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
24	The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
25	Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.

\section{Experiments}

\subsection{Setup}

We evaluate on synthetic and semi-synthetic data generating processes (DGPs); full specifications appear in Appendix~\ref{app:dgp}.
The synthetic DGP generates $N{=}5{,}000$ observations from a randomized trial with $K \in \{2, 4\}$ subgroups, controlled CATE heterogeneity $\Delta\tau$, and subgroup-specific symmetric misclassification rates with heterogeneity $\Delta\pi$.
Expert labels ($n_{\text{expert}} \in \{50, \ldots, 2000\}$) are a simple random sample with true $Z$ observed; each configuration is repeated for 100 Monte Carlo runs.
The semi-synthetic DGP samples $N{=}5{,}000$ tweets from TweetEval sentiment~\cite{barbieri2020tweeteval}, defining $K{=}4$ subgroups by crossing hashtag presence and text length (unbalanced: 39\%/38\%/12\%/11\%), with misclassification rates $\pi \in \{0.05, 0.10, 0.15, 0.25\}$ reflecting empirical evidence that text features degrade LLM accuracy~\cite{ashwin2025bias}.

We compare: (1) \textit{Naive} (no correction), (2) \textit{Global} (pooled confusion matrix), (3) \textit{Stratified MLE} (per-subgroup MLE without pooling), (4) \textit{HB EC-HTE} (our method), (5) \textit{PPCI}~\cite{sui2026ppci}, and (6) \textit{EC-HTE+PPCI}.
For CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, we compare naive, global, and EC-HTE variants.
Primary metrics are $|\text{bias}|$, RMSE, and 95\% CI coverage, averaged across subgroups and 100 MC runs.
Real-data validation on hate speech detection confirms $\Delta\pi = 0.117$ across text-feature subgroups (Appendix~\ref{app:hatespeech}).
The heterogeneity pattern persists across six OpenAI models spanning three generations (Appendix~\ref{app:multilm}).
EC-HTE maintains $\geq$94.5\% coverage under up to 50\% subgroup misspecification noise (Appendix~\ref{app:robustness}).

\subsection{Bias Mechanism Verification}
\label{sec:bias_mechanism}

The bias decomposition identity (Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}) predicts that global correction introduces bias proportional to $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ at the subgroup level.
We verify this identity empirically across 520 configurations spanning $K \in \{2,4\}$, two misclassification regimes, and six expert budget levels.
Regressing observed subgroup bias on the predicted $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product yields $R^2 = 0.994$ for $K{=}2$ and $R^2 = 0.974$ for $K{=}4$; the residual variance reflects MC sampling noise rather than model misspecification, since Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity} is an exact identity at the population level.
In 50\% of configurations (260/520, excluding $\Delta_c{=}0$ rows where bias is zero by construction), global correction produces larger absolute bias than the naive estimator.
The damage concentrates in low-$\pi$ subgroups: among subgroups where $\pi_s < \bar{\pi}$, global correction increases bias in 84.6\% of cases.
Maximum observed amplification reaches 2.86$\times$ (K=2) and 2.41$\times$ (K=4) relative to the naive estimator.
Figure~\ref{fig:heatmap} visualizes the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ amplification surface across the parameter grid.

(b) High-error subgroup: when $\Delta\pi > 0.12$ (dashed line), global correction \emph{increases} bias relative to the naive estimator (hatched region), with amplification reaching 2.86$\times$.}
\label{fig:heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{EC-HTE Evaluation}
\label{sec:ec_hte_eval}

Table~\ref{tab:main_results} presents the main results across representative configurations.
In the synthetic DGP with $K{=}2$ subgroups and extreme misclassification heterogeneity, HB EC-HTE reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.059 (global) to 0.011 (a 5.4$\times$ reduction) while maintaining nominal coverage (0.95) and comparable RMSE (0.093 vs.\ 0.099).
The advantage persists at $K{=}4$: EC-HTE achieves $|\text{bias}|{=}0.009$ versus 0.056 for global (6.2$\times$ reduction), though with a small RMSE penalty (0.127 vs.\ 0.125).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), global correction already achieves low bias (0.009), and EC-HTE reduces this to 0.005 but the difference is not statistically significant ($p > 0.05$; Appendix~\ref{app:mcse}), while RMSE is comparable (0.075 vs.\ 0.074).
Methods converge as expected when $\Delta\pi$ is small: the variance cost of stratification is not offset by bias reduction.

In the semi-synthetic TweetEval experiment, the pattern shifts.
Global correction achieves the lowest $|\text{bias}|$ (0.023) among non-oracle methods, while HB EC-HTE attains 0.027 with substantially higher RMSE (0.225 vs.\ 0.124).
This is consistent with moderate $\Delta\pi{=}0.20$ and the high-error subgroups (S2, S3) comprising only 23\% of data: the bias reduction from stratification is marginal while the variance cost of four per-subgroup confusion matrices is substantial.
HB EC-HTE does improve over stratified MLE (RMSE 0.225 vs.\ 0.248), confirming that partial pooling helps, but the improvement is insufficient to overcome the structural variance from unbalanced subgroup sizes.
At $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 250$, HB and MLE converge to within 5\% on all metrics.

\paragraph{CausalForest K-dependence.}
When the downstream estimator is a CausalForest~\cite{wager2018causal}, the bias mechanism operates with amplified magnitude.
At $K{=}4$/extreme/$n{=}500$, EC-HTE Forest reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.191 (global) to 0.040, a 4.8$\times$ improvement with dramatically better coverage (0.91 vs.\ 0.58).
The debiasing-hurts phenomenon intensifies: global correction amplifies naive bias by up to 5.9$\times$ in the worst subgroup, because the forest's sensitivity to covariate noise magnifies the effect of label errors.
At $K{=}4$/$n{=}100$, EC-HTE Forest RMSE reaches 1.43 (3.5$\times$ naive), underscoring the budget guidelines in Section~\ref{sec:budget}.

\subsection{Diagnostic Criterion}
\label{sec:diagnostic}

As a practical corollary of Theorem~\ref{thm:bias_identity}, the $\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau$ product provides a computable diagnostic for predicting when global correction will fail.
Using leave-one-out cross-validation at the subgroup level, a threshold classifier on $|\Delta\pi \times \Delta\tau|$ achieves AUC = 0.83 for predicting whether global correction increases bias relative to the naive estimator.
The Pearson correlation between the signed product and the observed bias ratio is $r = 0.86$.
At the setting level (averaging across subgroups within a configuration), the diagnostic has AUC = 0.47, which is no better than random.
The diagnostic operates at the subgroup level because the product criterion identifies \emph{which subgroups} are affected rather than whether a given experimental setting is globally problematic.
In practice, the diagnostic enables researchers to identify vulnerable subgroups before committing to a correction strategy: if any subgroup has $\pi_s \ll \bar{\pi}$ and $\tau(z)$ varies across $z$-levels, global correction should be avoided.
Figure~\ref{fig:roc} (Appendix) shows the ROC curve and correlation scatter plot.

\subsection{Expert Budget Analysis}
\label{sec:budget}

The crossover point at which EC-HTE achieves lower RMSE than global correction is $n_{\text{expert}} = 250$ for $K{=}2$/extreme and $n_{\text{expert}} = 1000$ for $K{=}4$/extreme (Figure~\ref{fig:budget} in the Appendix).
Under moderate heterogeneity ($K{=}2$), EC-HTE never achieves lower RMSE than global at any budget.
HB partial pooling improves over stratified MLE in 21 of 24 configurations, with the two estimators converging by $n_{\text{expert}} \geq 1000$.

\subsection{PPCI Complementarity}
\label{sec:ppci}

EC-HTE corrects covariate misclassification but cannot address outcome-level error; PPCI~\cite{sui2026ppci} corrects outcome-level error but assumes correct covariates.
Under both error types simultaneously (DGP~C), EC-HTE+PPCI reduces $|\text{bias}|$ from 0.179 to 0.007 ($z{=}0$), a $25\times$ improvement over EC-HTE alone (Table~\ref{tab:ppci} in the Appendix).
Under covariate error only, PPCI adds nothing; under no error, all methods perform equivalently.
The two corrections are complementary: EC-HTE handles covariate-side $M^{-1}$ inversion while PPCI handles residual outcome-level bias.
